title: Ἰκτῖνος καὶ ὄφις
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 135. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.l: A kite, having snatched up a snake, flew off.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ἐπιστραφεὶς καὶ δακὼν καὶ ἀμφότεροι ⟨ἐκ⟩ τοῦ ὕψους κατενεχθέντες, ὁ μὲν ἰκτῖνος ἐτεθνήκει· ὁ δὲ ὄφις ἔφη αὐτῷ· « Τί τοσοῦτον ἐμάνης, ὅτι τοὺς μηδὲν ἀδικοῦντας βλάπτειν ἠβούλου ;
sentences.tr: Ho de epistrapheis kai dakōn kai amphoteroi ⟨ek⟩ tou hypsous katenechthentes, ho men iktinos etethnēkei· ho de ophis ephē autōi· « Ti tosouton emanēs, hoti tous mēden adikountas blaptein ēboulou ;
sentences.l: And the other, having turned about and having bitten, and both of them having been carried down ⟨from⟩ the height, the kite was dead; but the snake said to him: « Why were you so mad, that you wanted to injure those who do no wrong?
sentences.i: And the snake turned about and bit, and both of them were carried down ⟨from⟩ the height; the kite lay dead, and the snake said to him: « Why were you so mad as to want to injure those who do no wrong?
sentences.n: The sentence never straightens out: ἐπιστραφείς, δακών and κατενεχθέντες are left as participles with no finite verb of their own, and the anacoluthon stands in Chambry's text unmended. Ὁ δέ is the snake, not the kite. ⟨ἐκ⟩ is Chambry's own supplement, marked by the angle brackets. ἐτεθνήκει is a pluperfect and states the condition, 'was dead', not the act of dying. μηδέν rather than οὐδέν with the participle makes the description general — such creatures as do no wrong.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ δίκην ἔδωκας τῆς ἁρπαγῆς δικαίαν. »
sentences.tr: alla dikēn edōkas tēs harpagēs dikaian. »
sentences.l: But you have paid a just penalty for your snatching. »
sentences.n: δίκην δοῦναι is the fixed phrase for paying a penalty, with the genitive naming the charge one pays it for. δίκη and δικαίαν side by side are the same root twice over: the penalty is justice, and it is just.

sentences.t: Ὅτι πλεονεξίᾳ τις προσέχων καὶ τοὺς ἀσθενεστέρους ἀδικῶν, ἰσχυροτέρῳ προσπεσών, ὡς οὐκ ἐλπίζει, ἐκτίσει τότε καὶ ἃ πρότερον ἐποίησε κακά.
sentences.tr: Hoti pleonexiāi tis prosechōn kai tous asthenesterous adikōn, ischyroterōi prospesōn, hōs ouk elpizei, ektisei tote kai ha proteron epoiēse kaka.
sentences.l: That one who gives himself to greed and wrongs those weaker, falling in with someone stronger, in a way he does not expect, will then pay for the evil deeds he did before as well.
sentences.i: The story shows that a man who gives himself to greed and wrongs those weaker than himself will, when he falls in with a stronger one in a way he does not expect, pay then for the evil he did before as well.
sentences.n: The introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek — Ὅτι stands as though “the story shows” had come before it — and is supplied in the idiomatic line. προσέχω with the dative is to hold oneself close to a thing, to be given over to it. ἐκτίνω is to pay a debt off in full. ὡς οὐκ ἐλπίζει says the reckoning comes from the quarter he was not watching.
